text: This case study is an illustrative, fictional scenario, not a report of a real incident. Eighteen months after Lesson 30's roadmap, an independent auditor scores Meridian Health Partners' zero trust rollout well against the CISA model -- Identity, Networks, Applications and Workloads, and Devices all at Advanced. The audit reads like a success story, because in almost every real sense, it is one.

Buried in the audit's scope notes is scope exclusion number four: ClaimFlow's legacy SFTP batch export, excluded because the vendor confirmed it was being replaced by the API gateway integration from Lesson 29 and scheduled for decommission within two quarters. That was a reasonable call the day it was written. But the old integration kept running during the migration, using a service account with read access to Meridian's entire shared folder structure -- never re-scoped, because it was already on the list to disappear.

The API migration slipped four months behind schedule, an ordinary kind of project delay. The SFTP export kept running the whole time, still excluded from the next audit cycle. A credential-stuffing campaign eventually turned up a reused password matching that service account -- which had no MFA, because it was a non-interactive scheduled job that the Conditional Access policy never covered. The attacker pulled the full shared-folder export, far more than claims data alone.

The checklist didn't fail to catch this -- scope exclusion four was a line item everyone agreed to, not a finding anyone missed. The real gap is that nothing automatically re-triggered a review when the decommission date slipped. An exemption with a deadline and no automatic re-check functions as an exemption with no deadline at all, and what an audit measures is never quite the same thing as what actually needs protecting.

Two fixes would have closed this gap without redesigning anything from Lessons 29 or 30. First, track every temporary exclusion as its own risk item with an owner and an expiration date, instead of a footnote that quietly vanishes from the next audit's scope. Second, apply assume-breach containment to excluded systems too -- scoping that service account down to only the claims folder it actually needed would have limited the damage even while it stayed outside the main identity fabric.

A system being out of an audit's scope should never mean it's out of scope for containment. That's the gap a checklist alone can't close, and it's the lesson this chapter's final review carries into Lesson 32, alongside everything else the Advanced Specialization stage built toward.
